claim: Cancer is a disease characterized by uncontrolled cell proliferation.
source: Cancer is a disease characterized by uncontrolled cell proliferation, but the precise pathological mechanisms underlying tumorigenesis often remain to be elucidated.
evidence: This is a well-established definition of cancer in the scientific literature.

claim: Condensates formed by phase separation have emerged as a new principle governing the organization and functional regulation of cells.
source: In recent years, condensates formed by phase separation have emerged as a new principle governing the organization and functional regulation of cells.
evidence: This statement reflects recent scientific consensus in the field of cell biology.

claim: Cancer-related mutations are linked to aberrantly altered condensate assembly.
source: Increasing evidence links cancer-related mutations to aberrantly altered condensate assembly, suggesting that condensates play a key role in tumorigenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by accumulating research findings in the field.

claim: Condensates play a key role in tumorigenesis.
source: Increasing evidence links cancer-related mutations to aberrantly altered condensate assembly, suggesting that condensates play a key role in tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the link between cancer mutations and condensate assembly.

claim: Cancer cells acquire the ability to evade growth suppressors.
source: In addition to sustaining proliferative signaling and an unlimited replicative potential, many cancers cells acquire the ability to evade growth suppressors, resist cell death, induce angiogenesis, and activate invasion and metastasis (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011.

claim: Cancer cells acquire the ability to resist cell death.
source: In addition to sustaining proliferative signaling and an unlimited replicative potential, many cancers cells acquire the ability to evade growth suppressors, resist cell death, induce angiogenesis, and activate invasion and metastasis (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011.

claim: Cancer cells acquire the ability to induce angiogenesis.
source: In addition to sustaining proliferative signaling and an unlimited replicative potential, many cancers cells acquire the ability to evade growth suppressors, resist cell death, induce angiogenesis, and activate invasion and metastasis (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011.

claim: Cancer cells acquire the ability to activate invasion and metastasis.
source: In addition to sustaining proliferative signaling and an unlimited replicative potential, many cancers cells acquire the ability to evade growth suppressors, resist cell death, induce angiogenesis, and activate invasion and metastasis (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011.

claim: Cancer cells interact with surrounding stromal cells and remodel the extracellular matrix to construct specific tumor microenvironments that support tumor growth and progression.
source: Moreover, cancer cells interact with surrounding stromal cell and remodel the extracellular matrix to construct specific tumor microenvironments that support tumor growth and progression (Egeblad et al., 2010; Kessenbrock et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Egeblad et al., 2010; Kessenbrock et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2012.

claim: Genomic instability is often crucial for tumorigenesis.
source: Of note, genomic instability raises the possibility to introduce genetic mutations, thus it is often crucial for tumorigenesis (Jeggo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jeggo et al., 2016.

claim: Genetic mutations in cancer-related genes frequently lead to the dysregulation of oncogene activity or inhibit the activity of a tumor suppressor gene.
source: The genetic mutations in cancer-related genes frequently lead to the dysregulation of oncogene activity or they inhibit the activity of a tumor suppressor gene, which then drive the oncogenic process forward.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cancer biology.

claim: The precise pathological mechanisms underlying tumorigenesis are still largely unclear.
source: Although significant progress has been made in identifying driver mutations and associated oncogenic processes and pathways, the precise pathological mechanisms underlying tumorigenesis are still largely unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Cells possess various membraneless compartments, including nucleoli, Cajal bodies, and promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML) bodies in the nucleus.
source: In addition to the classical membrane-bound organelles, such as the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, cells possess various membraneless compartments, including nucleoli, Cajal bodies, and promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML) bodies in the nucleus (Sawyer et al., 2019) as well as stress granules (SGs) or processing bodies (P bodies) in the cytoplasm (Banani et al., 2017; Jain et al., 2016; Sachdev et al., 2019; Wheeler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sawyer et al., 2019.

claim: Cells possess membraneless compartments including stress granules (SGs) or processing bodies (P bodies) in the cytoplasm.
source: In addition to the classical membrane-bound organelles, such as the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, cells possess various membraneless compartments, including nucleoli, Cajal bodies, and promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML) bodies in the nucleus (Sawyer et al., 2019) as well as stress granules (SGs) or processing bodies (P bodies) in the cytoplasm (Banani et al., 2017; Jain et al., 2016; Sachdev et al., 2019; Wheeler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017; Jain et al., 2016; Sachdev et al., 2019; Wheeler et al., 2016.

claim: The assembly of membraneless compartments is often driven by a physical process known as phase separation.
source: Recent studies suggest that the assembly of these membraneless compartments is often driven by a physical process known as phase separation (Banani et al., 2017; Boeynaems et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017; Boeynaems et al., 2018.

claim: Biomolecular condensates have no fixed stoichiometry.
source: In contrast to other types of assemblies, condensates have no fixed stoichiometry, they are able to concentrate molecules, and frequently form through phase separation.
evidence: This is a defining characteristic of condensates based on current understanding.

claim: Condensates are able to concentrate molecules.
source: In contrast to other types of assemblies, condensates have no fixed stoichiometry, they are able to concentrate molecules, and frequently form through phase separation.
evidence: This is a defining characteristic of condensates based on current understanding.

claim: Condensates frequently form through phase separation.
source: In contrast to other types of assemblies, condensates have no fixed stoichiometry, they are able to concentrate molecules, and frequently form through phase separation.
evidence: This is a defining characteristic of condensates based on current understanding.

claim: Phase separation is a process by which a well-mixed solution of macromolecules spontaneously separates into two phases: a dense and a dilute phase.
source: Phase separation is a process by which a well-mixed solution of macromolecules such as proteins or nucleic acids spontaneously separates into two phases: a dense and a dilute phase.
evidence: This is a definition of phase separation based on established physical chemistry principles.

claim: The dense phase has liquid-like properties and enriches certain macromolecules while others are depleted.
source: The dense phase has liquid-like properties and enriches certain macromolecules while others are depleted, allowing the dense phase to function as a compartment (Alberti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alberti et al., 2019.

claim: Liquid condensates can mature into more solid-like states after their formation by phase separation.
source: After their formation by phase separation, liquid condensates can mature into more solid-like states.
evidence: This describes a known property of condensates based on research findings.

claim: Condensates can adopt a range of different material properties, from dynamic liquid-like droplets to non-dynamic gels and solid amyloids.
source: They can thus adopt a range of different material properties, from dynamic liquid-like droplets to non-dynamic gels and solid amyloids (Woodruff et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Woodruff et al., 2018.

claim: Proper condensate formation is essential for homeostasis as it provides cells with spatiotemporal control over protein function.
source: Proper condensate formation is essential for homeostasis as it provides cells with spatiotemporal control over protein function.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional roles of condensates in cellular processes.

claim: Abnormal or aberrant condensates can form under conditions such as chronic stress, aging, or disease-associated mutations.
source: Under some conditions, such as chronic stress, aging, or disease-associated mutations, abnormal or aberrant condensates can form.
evidence: This is based on observations from various disease contexts.

claim: Phase separation of crystallin proteins in the eye lens causes opacification and visual impairment.
source: Early research focused on cataracts, showing that phase separation of crystallin proteins in the eye lens causes opacification and thus visual impairment (Siezen and Benedek, 1985; Siezen et al., 1985; Tanaka et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Siezen and Benedek, 1985; Siezen et al., 1985; Tanaka et al., 1977.

claim: Excess accumulation of aberrant crystallin condensates during ageing was proposed to drive the formation of cataracts.
source: Excess accumulation of aberrant crystallin condensates during ageing was proposed to drive the formation of cataracts (Benedek, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Benedek, 1997.

claim: Aberrant phase transitions are involved in neurodegenerative diseases, affecting neuronal proteins such as Fused in Sarcoma (FUS) in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS).
source: Recent studies showed that such aberrant phase transitions are also involved in neurodegenerative diseases, affecting neuronal proteins such as Fused in Sarcoma (FUS) in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) (Patel et al., 2015), Tau in Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Wegmann et al., 2018) and huntingtin exon 1 in Huntington's disease (HD) (Peskett et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Patel et al., 2015.

claim: Aberrant phase transitions are involved in neurodegenerative diseases, affecting Tau in Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Recent studies showed that such aberrant phase transitions are also involved in neurodegenerative diseases, affecting neuronal proteins such as Fused in Sarcoma (FUS) in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) (Patel et al., 2015), Tau in Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Wegmann et al., 2018) and huntingtin exon 1 in Huntington's disease (HD) (Peskett et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wegmann et al., 2018.

claim: Aberrant phase transitions are involved in neurodegenerative diseases, affecting huntingtin exon 1 in Huntington's disease (HD).
source: Recent studies showed that such aberrant phase transitions are also involved in neurodegenerative diseases, affecting neuronal proteins such as Fused in Sarcoma (FUS) in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) (Patel et al., 2015), Tau in Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Wegmann et al., 2018) and huntingtin exon 1 in Huntington's disease (HD) (Peskett et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peskett et al., 2018.

claim: Patient mutations in FUS accelerate a transition of reconstituted FUS droplets from a liquid to a solid-like state.
source: For example, patient mutations in FUS were shown to accelerate a transition of reconstituted FUS droplets from a liquid to a solid-like state (Patel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Patel et al., 2015.

claim: Hardening of FUS condensates is associated with the formation of supramolecular FUS fibrils that have properties of amyloid-like aggregates.
source: This hardening of FUS condensates is associated with the formation of supramolecular FUS fibrils that have properties of amyloid-like aggregates.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of FUS droplet hardening and fibril formation.

claim: Phase separation requires the establishment of a network of interactions through multivalent protein molecules.
source: Recent work shows that phase separation requires the establishment of a network of interactions through multivalent protein molecules.
evidence: This is based on recent research findings in the field.

claim: Multivalent interactions are promoted by proteins containing multiple-folded modular domains or intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) or oligomerization domains.
source: These multivalent interactions are promoted by proteins containing multiple-folded modular domains or intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) (Gomes and Shorter, 2019) or oligomerization domains (Dao et al., 2018; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gomes and Shorter, 2019 and Dao et al., 2018, and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Phase-separating proteins containing polymerizing domains such as the DIX domain assemble into filaments that are crosslinked into three-dimensional condensates.
source: Another class of phase-separating proteins containing polymerizing domains such as the DIX domain, which assemble into filaments that are crosslinked into three-dimensional condensates (Bienz, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bienz, 2020.

claim: Phase separation by proteins with folded modular domains was first established for two interacting proteins containing multiple copies of the SRC homology 3 (SH3) domains or the SH3 ligand proline-rich motifs (PRM).
source: Phase separation by proteins with folded modular domains was first established for two interacting proteins containing multiple copies of the SRC homology 3 (SH3) domains or the SH3 ligand proline-rich motifs (PRM) (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: Phase separation by multiple SH3 containing protein NCK and multiple PRM containing protein N-WASP promoted Arp2/3-mediated actin assembly.
source: The study further demonstrated condensate formation by a three-component system containing the proteins nephrin, NCK, and neural Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (N-WASP), and showed that phase separation by multiple SH3 containing protein NCK and multiple PRM containing protein N-WASP promoted Arp2/3-mediated actin assembly (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: Multivalent interactions among multi-domain proteins underlie the formation of membrane-associated phase-separated signaling clusters by T cell receptor (TCR) components.
source: Multivalent interactions among multi-domain proteins were also shown to underlie the formation of membrane-associated phase-separated signaling clusters by T cell receptor (TCR) components (Ditlev et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Su et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ditlev et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Su et al., 2016.

claim: Folded modular domains are often connected by intrinsically disordered linker sequences that determine the material properties of the formed condensates.
source: The folded modular domains are often connected by intrinsically disordered linker sequences that determine the material properties of the formed condensates (Harmon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harmon et al., 2017.

claim: IDRs often harbor multiple short amino acid motifs that mediate weak interactions, called stickers.
source: Although IDRs lack a defined three-dimensional structure, they often harbor multiple short amino acid motifs that mediate weak interactions. These motifs have been called stickers because of their adhesive properties (Martin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Martin et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: The driving forces for sticker-mediated interactions are π-π stacking, cation-π interactions, or charge-charge interactions.
source: The driving forces for sticker-mediated interactions are π-π stacking, cation-π interactions, or charge-charge interactions (Nott et al., 2015; Vernon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nott et al., 2015; Vernon et al., 2018.

claim: Mutations in spacer residues in FUS changed the material properties of FUS condensates: glycine residues enhanced droplet fluidity, whereas glutamine and serine residues promoted hardening.
source: For instance, mutations in spacer residues in FUS changed the material properties of FUS condensates: glycine residues enhanced droplet fluidity, whereas glutamine and serine residues promoted hardening (Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: Low-complexity domains (LCDs) are IDRs that are enriched for only a few amino acids.
source: IDRs that are enriched for only a few amino acids are referred to as low-complexity domains (LCDs) (Boeynaems et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Boeynaems et al., 2018.

claim: Prion-like domains (PLDs) are LCDs that contain polar, uncharged amino acid residues and show compositional similarity to yeast prion domains.
source: A subset of LCDs contains polar, uncharged amino acid residues, such as glutamine (Gln), asparagine (Asn), serine (Ser), or tyrosine (Tyr), and shows a compositional similarity to yeast prion domains (Alberti et al., 2009). These LCDs are referred to as prion-like domains (PLDs) and often found in RNA-binding proteins (RBPs).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alberti et al., 2009.

claim: PLDs are often found in RNA-binding proteins (RBPs).
source: These LCDs are referred to as prion-like domains (PLDs) and often found in RNA-binding proteins (RBPs).
evidence: This is an observation from the literature.

claim: PLDs can assemble into self-templating protein aggregates with infectious properties.
source: Proteins with PLDs have initially gained attention because of their ability to assemble into self-templating protein aggregates. These aggregates can have infectious properties, as they can spread between cells, tissues and sometimes individuals (Chakravarty and Jarosz, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chakravarty and Jarosz, 2018.

claim: The isolated PLDs of FUS, hnRNPA1, and FCA can assemble into condensates at high concentrations in vitro.
source: For example, the isolated PLDs of FUS (Burke et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2017), heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A1 (hnRNPA1) (Kim et al., 2013) and flowering control locus A (FCA) (Fang et al., 2019) can assemble into condensates at high concentrations in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burke et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2013; Fang et al., 2019.

claim: Phase separation of the FUS proteins requires collective interactions among tyrosine residues in the PLD and arginine residues in the RNA-binding domain (RBD).
source: For example, phase separation of the FUS proteins was shown to require collective interactions among tyrosine residues in the PLD and arginine residues in the RNA-binding domain (RBD) (Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018a.

claim: Phase separation of the PLD-containing poly(A)-binding protein (Pab1 in yeast) is not mediated by its PLD, but by the RNA recognition motifs (RRMs).
source: Moreover, phase separation of the PLD-containing poly(A)-binding protein (Pab1 in yeast) is not mediated by its PLD, but by the RNA recognition motifs (RRMs). Rather, the PLD modulates condensate formation by the Pab1 RRM domains under heat shock condition (Riback et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riback et al., 2017.

claim: UBQLN2 oligomerizes via the folded STI1-II domain and this promotes UBQLN2 phase separation.
source: For example, UBQLN2, an adaptor protein required for cellular protein quality control, oligomerizes via the folded STI1-II domain and this promotes UBQLN2 phase separation (Dao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dao et al., 2018.

claim: Phase separation is often regulated by post-translational modifications (PTMs).
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that phase separation is often regulated by post-translational modifications (PTMs) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on accumulating evidence in the field and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: PTMs, including phosphorylation, acetylation, arginine methylation, and SUMOylation, have been implicated in the assembly and disassembly of condensates.
source: PTMs, including phosphorylation, acetylation, arginine methylation, and SUMOylation, have been implicated in the assembly and disassembly of condensates, as well as the regulation of their material properties (Hofweber and Dormann, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hofweber and Dormann, 2019.

claim: Lysine acetylation regulates phase separation of the microtubule-binding protein Tau.
source: For example, recent studies showed that lysine acetylation regulates phase separation of the microtubule-binding protein Tau (Carlomagno et al., 2017; Ferreon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carlomagno et al., 2017; Ferreon et al., 2018.

claim: Phosphorylation of serine residues or methylation of arginine residues can suppress phase separation of FUS.
source: Moreover, phosphorylation of serine residues or methylation of arginine residues can suppress phase separation of FUS (Hofweber et al., 2018; Monahan et al., 2017; Qamar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hofweber et al., 2018; Monahan et al., 2017; Qamar et al., 2018.

claim: Many disease-associated mutations in FUS are adjacent to or directly affect amino acids that are modified by PTMs.
source: These PTMs may play an important role in the formation of pathological FUS aggregates, because many disease-associated mutations in FUS are adjacent to or directly affect amino acids that are modified by PTMs.
evidence: This is an observation about the location of disease mutations relative to PTM sites.

claim: Phosphorylation of the RNA polymerase II (Pol II) C-terminal domain prevents the partitioning of Pol II into transcription initiation condensates but promotes partitioning into splicing condensates.
source: For example, phosphorylation of the RNA polymerase II (Pol II) C-terminal domain prevents the partitioning of Pol II into transcription initiation condensates but it promotes partitioning into splicing condensates (Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2019.

claim: Sumoylation of SOP-2 results in an increase in both size and number of condensates in comparison to the unmodified protein.
source: For instance, sumoylation of SOP-2 results in an increase in both size and number of condensates in comparison to the unmodified protein (Qu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Qu et al., 2020.

claim: DYRK3 localizes to condensates and phosphorylates multiple serine and threonine residues within IDRs.
source: One example is the dual specificity tyrosine-phosphorylation regulated kinase 3 (DYRK3). DYRK3 localizes to condensates and phosphorylates multiple serine and threonine residues within IDRs (Rai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rai et al., 2018.

claim: DYRK3 kinase activity is essential for regulating disassembly of SG during stress recovery.
source: DYRK3 kinase activity is essential for regulating disassembly of SG during stress recovery (Wippich et al., 2013), and it acts as a dissolvase of many additional membraneless condensates during mitosis (Rai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wippich et al., 2013.

claim: DYRK3 acts as a dissolvase of many membraneless condensates during mitosis.
source: DYRK3 kinase activity is essential for regulating disassembly of SG during stress recovery (Wippich et al., 2013), and it acts as a dissolvase of many additional membraneless condensates during mitosis (Rai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rai et al., 2018.

claim: RNA is a ligand of many phase-separating RBPs and it often regulates RBP phase behavior.
source: For instance, RNA is a ligand of many phase-separating RBPs and it often regulates RBP phase behavior.
evidence: This is based on observations from multiple studies.

claim: The effect of RNA on RBP phase separation is concentration-dependent: low amounts of RNA often promote phase separation, whereas high amounts can inhibit it.
source: The effect of RNA on RBP phase separation is concentration-dependent: low amounts of RNA often promote phase separation, whereas high amounts can inhibit it (Maharana et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maharana et al., 2018.

claim: ncRNA NEAT1 is essential for paraspeckle assembly.
source: One example is ncRNA NEAT1, which is essential for paraspeckle assembly (Yamazaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamazaki et al., 2018.

claim: ncRNAs play important regulatory roles in different cancer-related cellular processes and pathways.
source: More generally, ncRNAs play important regulatory roles in different cancer-related cellular processes and pathways (Anastasiadou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anastasiadou et al., 2018.

claim: PAR chains promote the condensation of FUS at low concentrations in vitro.
source: PAR chains are chemically similar to RNA and they promote the condensation of FUS at low concentrations in vitro (Patel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Patel et al., 2015.

claim: Synthesis of PAR chains at the DNA sites is required for the recruitment of FUS and the formation of DNA damage condensates in cells.
source: Synthesis of PAR chains at the DNA sites is also required for the recruitment of FUS and the formation of DNA damage condensates in cells (Altmeyer et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Altmeyer et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015.

claim: Aberrant PAR assembly has been linked to many forms of cancer.
source: Critically, aberrant PAR assembly has been linked to many forms of cancer (Hou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hou et al., 2019.

claim: Phase separation of the m6A-binding proteins YTHDF1, YTHDF2, and YTHDF3 was markedly enhanced by multiple m6A modifications on mRNA.
source: Phase separation of the m6A-binding proteins YTHDF1, YTHDF2, and YTHDF3 was markedly enhanced by multiple m6A modifications on mRNA (Gao et al., 2019; Ries et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2019; Ries et al., 2019.

claim: m6A modification of mRNA enhances mRNA partitioning into different condensates.
source: Moreover, m6A modification of mRNA further enhances mRNA partitioning into different condensates.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of m6A modifications on phase separation.

claim: Dysregulation of RNA modifications is closely associated with various human cancers.
source: Emerging evidence also suggests that dysregulation of RNA modifications is closely associated with various human cancers (Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2020.

claim: Phase separation of proteins can be used to sense changes in the environment and mount adequate adaptive responses.
source: For instance, it has been proposed that phase separation of proteins can be used to sense changes in the environment and that the formed condensates then mount adequate adaptive responses.
evidence: This is a proposed function based on observations of phase behavior.

claim: Phase separation of Pab1 has been observed in response to thermal stress and changes in cytosolic pH.
source: For example, phase separation of Pab1 has been observed in response to thermal stress and changes in cytosolic pH (Riback et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Riback et al., 2017.

claim: Condensation of Sup35 is induced by an energy depletion-induced acidification of the cytosol.
source: In addition, condensation of Sup35 is induced by an energy depletion-induced acidification of the cytosol (Franzmann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Franzmann et al., 2018.

claim: The RNA-binding protein Pbp1 senses the cellular redox state and forms condensates under reducing conditions.
source: Another example is the RNA-binding protein Pbp1, which senses the cellular redox state and forms condensates under reducing conditions (Kato et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kato et al., 2019.

claim: Pbp1 condensates are able to sequester and inactivate TORC1, thus coupling the metabolic redox state to TOR signaling.
source: For example, Pbp1 condensates are able to sequester and inactivate TORC1, thus coupling the metabolic redox state to TOR signaling (Kato et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kato et al., 2019.

claim: Condensates can accelerate biochemical reaction kinetics by increasing the specific activity of reactants inside condensates.
source: Condensates have also been shown to accelerate biochemical reaction kinetics by increasing the specific activity of reactants inside condensates.
evidence: This is based on observations from multiple studies.

claim: The formation of miRNA-induced silencing complex (miRISC) condensates is associated with increased deadenylation activity.
source: For example, the formation of miRNA-induced silencing complex (miRISC) condensates is associated with increased deadenylation activity (Sheu-Gruttadauria and MacRae, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sheu-Gruttadauria and MacRae, 2018.

claim: P bodies have been proposed to be reservoirs for translationally repressed mRNAs.
source: For instance, P bodies have been proposed to be reservoirs for translationally repressed mRNAs (Hubstenberger et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hubstenberger et al., 2017.

claim: Super-enhancers are clusters of several hundred enhancers bound cooperatively by transcription factors to drive robust transcription of genes for defining cell identity.
source: For example, super-enhancers, which are clusters of several hundred enhancers, are bound cooperatively by transcription factors to drive robust transcription of genes for defining cell identity (Hnisz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hnisz et al., 2013.

claim: Transcriptional coactivators and the mediator complex form condensates at super-enhancers, which may help to compartmentalize and concentrate the transcription apparatus.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that transcriptional coactivators and the mediator complex form condensates at super-enhancers, which may help to compartmentalize and concentrate the transcription apparatus (Boija et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2018; Sabari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boija et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2018; Sabari et al., 2018.

claim: Condensation by endocytic proteins can deform the plasma membrane and drive membrane invagination.
source: Notably, Michnick and colleagues demonstrated that condensation by endocytic proteins can deform the plasma membrane and drive membrane invagination (Michnick et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Michnick et al., 2019.

claim: Phase separation can buffer protein concentration noise.
source: Very recent evidence also suggests that phase separation can buffer protein concentration noise (Klosin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Klosin et al., 2020.

claim: The interaction among STT complex sorting factors and Tat substrate protein induces the formation of condensates, which is critical for Tat protein transport across the stroma to thylakoid membranes.
source: In chloroplasts, the interaction among STT complex sorting factors and Tat substrate protein induces the formation of condensates, which is critical for Tat protein transport across the stroma to thylakoid membranes (Ouyang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ouyang et al., 2020.

claim: Under stress conditions, some misfolded proteins accumulate in the granular component (GC) phase of the nucleolus, which prevents irreversible aggregation of misfolded proteins, facilitating refolding during recovery from stress.
source: Under stress conditions, some misfolded proteins accumulate in the granular component (GC) phase of the nucleolus, which prevents irreversible aggregation of misfolded proteins, facilitating refolding during recovery from stress (Frottin et al., 2019; Mediani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frottin et al., 2019; Mediani et al., 2019.

claim: Phase separation has been shown to be critical for the formation of proteasome-containing foci and the assembly of the autophagosome.
source: Phase separation has also been shown to be critical for the formation of proteasome-containing foci and the assembly of the autophagosome (Fujioka et al., 2020; Yasuda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fujioka et al., 2020; Yasuda et al., 2020.

claim: SPOP functions as a substrate adaptor of the cullin3 (CUL3)-RING ubiquitin ligase complex.
source: The tumor suppressor SPOP functions as a substrate adaptor of the cullin3 (CUL3)-RING ubiquitin ligase complex, which is frequently mutated in prostate cancer (Barbieri et al., 2012; Le Gallo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barbieri et al., 2012; Le Gallo et al., 2012.

claim: SPOP is frequently mutated in prostate cancer.
source: The tumor suppressor SPOP functions as a substrate adaptor of the cullin3 (CUL3)-RING ubiquitin ligase complex, which is frequently mutated in prostate cancer (Barbieri et al., 2012; Le Gallo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barbieri et al., 2012; Le Gallo et al., 2012.

claim: Tumor-associated missense mutations in the substrate recognition domain of SPOP disrupt substrate binding and ubiquitination, leading to the accumulation of oncogenic substrates.
source: Tumor-associated missense mutations in the substrate recognition domain of SPOP disrupt substrate binding and ubiquitination, leading to the accumulation of oncogenic substrates, such as steroid receptor coactivator (SRC3), c-MYC (Geng et al., 2017) and death-domain-associated protein (DAXX) (Kwon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Geng et al., 2017 and Kwon et al., 2006.

claim: Multivalent interactions between SPOP oligomers and motifs in oncogenic substrate proteins drive phase separation in vitro.
source: Bouchard et al. found that multivalent interactions between SPOP oligomers and motifs in oncogenic substrate proteins drive phase separation in vitro.
evidence: This is based on findings from Bouchard et al.

claim: Substrate proteins such as DAXX appear to be ubiquitylated inside the SPOP condensates in a CUL3-dependent manner.
source: Importantly, substrate proteins such as DAXX appear to be ubiquitylated inside the condensates in a CUL3-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an observation from the study of SPOP condensates.

claim: Cancer-associated SPOP mutations disrupt SPOP interaction with the substrates, causing a failure to form condensates, ubiquitylate the substrates and promote their degradation.
source: Consequently, cancer-associated SPOP mutations disrupt SPOP interaction with the substrates, causing a failure to form condensates, ubiquitylate the substrates and promote their degradation (Bouchard et al., 2018; Table 1 and Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bouchard et al., 2018 and illustrated in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: PARP1 synthesizes long PAR chains at DNA damage sites and plays a key role in DDR.
source: PARP1 synthesizes long PAR chains at DNA damage sites and plays a key role in DDR and PARP-1 has been ascribed diverse pro- or anti-tumorigenic roles (Weaver and Yang, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weaver and Yang, 2013.

claim: The formation of PAR chains initiates the formation of DNA damage condensates via recruitment and assembly of FET proteins (FUS, EWS, and TAF15).
source: The formation of PAR chains was shown to initiate the formation of DNA damage condensates via recruitment and assembly of FET proteins (FUS, EWS, and TAF15) (Altmeyer et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Table 1; Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Altmeyer et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015 and illustrated in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: 53BP1 drives the formation of a DNA damage repair compartment through phase separation in response to DNA damage.
source: Recently, 53BP1 was reported to drive the formation of a DNA damage repair compartment through phase separation in response to DNA damage, which was promoted by damage-induced long non-coding RNAs (dilncRNA) synthesized at DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) (Kilic et al., 2019; Pessina et al., 2019; Table 1 and Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kilic et al., 2019; Pessina et al., 2019 and illustrated in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Blocking dilncRNA transcription or inhibiting DNA repair condensate assembly through the chemical 1,6-hexanediol both led to a reduction in the efficiency of DNA repair.
source: Blocking dilncRNA transcription or inhibiting DNA repair condensate assembly through the chemical 1,6-hexanediol both led to a reduction in the efficiency of DNA repair, suggesting that 53BP1 repair compartment assembly is required for DSB repair (Pessina et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pessina et al., 2019.

claim: 53BP1 repair compartment assembly is required for DSB repair.
source: Blocking dilncRNA transcription or inhibiting DNA repair condensate assembly through the chemical 1,6-hexanediol both led to a reduction in the efficiency of DNA repair, suggesting that 53BP1 repair compartment assembly is required for DSB repair (Pessina et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing reduced repair efficiency when condensate assembly is blocked.

claim: DNA damage repair condensates recruit downstream effectors, such as p53 and the p53 co-activator USP28, which stabilizes p53 upon DNA damage.
source: Importantly, these DNA damage repair condensates recruit downstream effectors, such as p53 and the p53 co-activator USP28, which stabilizes p53 upon DNA damage.
evidence: This is based on observations of protein recruitment to DNA damage condensates.

claim: Disruption of DNA damage repair compartments led to impaired p53 induction and diminished p53 target gene expression as well as cell cycle arrest.
source: As a consequence, disruption of DNA damage repair compartments led to impaired p53 induction and diminished p53 target gene expression as well as cell cycle arrest (Kilic et al., 2019; Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kilic et al., 2019 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: 53BP1 is excluded from DNA damage condensates formed by FET proteins.
source: Intriguingly, 53BP1 is excluded from above-mentioned DNA damage condensates (Altmeyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Altmeyer et al., 2015.

claim: 53BP1 is recruited to DNA damage sites later than FET proteins.
source: Given that 53BP1 is recruited to DNA damage sites later (Aleksandrov et al., 2018), this suggests that cells can assemble DNA damage condensates with different compositions and presumably also functions (Altmeyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aleksandrov et al., 2018.

claim: Cells can assemble DNA damage condensates with different compositions and functions.
source: Given that 53BP1 is recruited to DNA damage sites later (Aleksandrov et al., 2018), this suggests that cells can assemble DNA damage condensates with different compositions and presumably also functions (Altmeyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of different protein compositions at different times.

claim: Cancer-associated translocations in FET proteins impair the cellular ability to interact with PAR chains, which may affect the assembly of condensates at DNA damage sites and thus undermine genome integrity.
source: These studies suggest that condensate assembly is intimately linked to the maintenance of genome stability. Indeed, cancer-associated translocations in FET proteins appear to impair the cellular ability to interact with PAR chains, which may affect the assembly of condensates at DNA damage sites and thus undermine genome integrity (Altmeyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Altmeyer et al., 2015 and involves speculation about the consequences.

claim: EWS-FLI1 is an oncogenic transcription factor that plays key roles in Ewing's sarcoma tumorigenesis.
source: EWS-FLI1 is an oncogenic transcription factor that plays key roles in Ewing's sarcoma tumorigenesis (Delattre et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Delattre et al., 1992.

claim: EWS-FLI1 is generated by a chromosomal translocation, in which a large portion of the prion-like domain (PLD) of EWSR1 is fused to the transcription factor FLI1 in Ewing's sarcoma.
source: This oncogenic factor is generated by a chromosomal translocation, in which a large portion of the prion-like domain (PLD) of EWSR1 is fused to the transcription factor FLI1 in Ewing's sarcoma (Tan and Manley, 2009; Toretsky and Wright, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tan and Manley, 2009; Toretsky and Wright, 2014.

claim: The translocated PLD of EWSR1 is essential for recruiting the BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) chromatin-remodeling complex to tumor-specific enhancers, activating an aberrant transcriptional cascade underlying Ewing sarcoma progression.
source: Rivera, Kadoch, and colleagues demonstrated that the translocated PLD was essential for recruiting the BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) chromatin-remodeling complex to tumor-specific enhancers, activating an aberrant transcriptional cascades that is underlying Ewing sarcoma progression (Boulay et al., 2017; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boulay et al., 2017 and listed in Table 1.

claim: EWS-FLI1 forms numerous nuclear foci, whereas FLI1 exhibits a more diffuse pattern.
source: Moreover, EWS-FLI1 forms numerous nuclear foci, whereas FLI1 exhibits a more diffuse pattern (Boulay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boulay et al., 2017.

claim: The aberrant transcriptional program in Ewing sarcoma is driven by aberrant condensate formation of EWS-FLI1.
source: The hypothesis was put forward that this transcriptional program is driven by aberrant condensate formation of EWS-FLI1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation of nuclear foci formation.

claim: Master transcription factors and the mediator coactivator use their disordered regions to form condensates at super-enhancers, which recruit Pol II to activate transcription sites.
source: Evidence is now also emerging that master transcription factors and the mediator coactivator use their disordered regions to form condensates at super-enhancers, which recruit Pol II to activate transcription sites (Boija et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2018; Sabari et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boija et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2018; Sabari et al., 2018.

claim: In some cancer cells, genomic alterations promote the formation of super-enhancers at oncogenes, which promote oncogenic transcriptional programs.
source: In some cancer cells, genomic alterations promote the formation of super-enhancers at oncogenes, which promote oncogenic transcriptional programs (Sengupta and George, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sengupta and George, 2017.

claim: Aberrant condensation at super-enhancers might be a general mechanism that cancer cells use to sustain high oncogene expression levels.
source: Thus, aberrant condensation at super-enhancers might be a general mechanism that cancer cells use to sustain high oncogene expression levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of super-enhancer formation at oncogenes in cancer cells.

claim: YAP and TAZ have been linked to tissue growth, stem cell activity, and tumorigenesis.
source: YAP and TAZ have been linked to tissue growth, stem cell activity, and tumorigenesis (Moya and Halder, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moya and Halder, 2019.

claim: YAP and TAZ bind to a subset of highly active enhancers and super-enhancers to drive the transcription of cell proliferation genes.
source: They bind to a subset of highly active enhancers and super-enhancers to drive the transcription of cell proliferation genes (Galli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galli et al., 2015.

claim: YAP and TAZ are pervasively activated in cancers.
source: Consequently, YAP and TAZ are pervasively activated in cancers (Zanconato et al., 2016; Zanconato et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zanconato et al., 2016; Zanconato et al., 2019.

claim: Activation of YAP in tumor-surrounding cells can suppress liver cancer in mice.
source: For example, activation of YAP in tumor-surrounding cells can suppress liver cancer in mice (Moya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moya et al., 2019.

claim: YAP and TAZ assemble into condensates in vitro and in vivo.
source: Recent evidence shows that YAP and TAZ assemble into condensates in vitro and in vivo (Cai et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2020; Table 1 and Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cai et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2020 and illustrated in Table 1 and Figure 4.

claim: YAP assembles into condensates at super-enhancer regions and these nuclear condensates contain TAZ and the transcription factor TEAD1.
source: In cells, YAP assembles into condensates at super-enhancer regions and these nuclear condensates contain TAZ but also the transcription factor TEAD1.
evidence: This is based on observations of YAP condensate composition in cells.

claim: YAP condensates recruit RNA polymerase II to trigger the transcription of proliferative genes.
source: These condensates appear to recruit RNA polymerase II to trigger the transcription of proliferative genes (Cai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cai et al., 2019.

claim: YAP and TAZ mutants defective in condensate formation displayed reduced transcriptional activity.
source: Furthermore, YAP and TAZ mutants defective in condensate formation, displayed reduced transcriptional activity, suggesting that transcriptional activity of YAP and TAZ is associated with their ability to assemble into condensates (Cai et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cai et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2020.

claim: TAZ-containing condensates are negatively regulated by Hippo signaling and sensitive to mechanical signals.
source: Importantly, TAZ-containing condensates are negatively regulated by Hippo signaling and sensitive to mechanical signals (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: YAP and TAZ could function as mechanotransducers, which detect a broad range of mechanical signals and convert them into cell-specific transcriptional responses.
source: In agreement with this, a growing body of evidence suggests that YAP and TAZ could function as mechanotransducers, which detect a broad range of mechanical signals and convert them into cell-specific transcriptional responses (Panciera et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Panciera et al., 2017.

claim: TAZ forms nuclear condensates in breast cancer tissue, in contrast to its diffuse localization in normal breast tissue.
source: Notably, in contrast to its diffuse localization in normal breast tissue, TAZ forms nuclear condensates in breast cancer tissue (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: CBX2 assembles into condensates that recruited the core subunits of the CBX2-PRC1 complex and directed the condensation of DNA and nucleosomes.
source: Chromobox 2 (CBX2), one subunit of Polycomb repressive complex 1 (PRC1), was recently shown to assemble into condensates that recruited the core subunits of the CBX2-PRC1 complex and directed the condensation of DNA and nucleosomes (Plys et al., 2019; Tatavosian et al., 2019; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Plys et al., 2019; Tatavosian et al., 2019 and listed in Table 1.

claim: PRC1 condensates contribute to chromatin compaction, thus repressing the expression of PRC1 target genes.
source: These studies suggest that PRC1 condensates contribute to chromatin compaction, thus repressing the expression of PRC1 target genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of DNA and nucleosome condensation by PRC1.

claim: Phase separation of phosphorylated nephrin receptor together with its downstream effector molecules NCK and N-WASP promotes actin assembly.
source: For instance, phase separation of phosphorylated nephrin receptor together with its downstream effector molecules NCK and N-WASP promotes actin assembly.
evidence: This is based on observations from studies of membrane receptor signaling.

claim: Enhancement of actin assembly by nephrin/NCK/N-WASP phase separation was linked to the longer membrane dwell time of N-WASP in these clusters.
source: This enhancement of actin assembly was linked to the longer membrane dwell time of N-WASP in these clusters.
evidence: This is inferred from experimental observations.

claim: Signaling condensates formed from the phosphorylated scaffold protein LAT and its two adaptors GRB2 and SOS promoted Ras activation by increasing membrane dwell time of SOS.
source: Similarly, signaling condensates formed from the phosphorylated scaffold protein linker for activation of T cells (LAT) and its two adaptors growth factor receptor-bound protein 2 (GRB2) and Son of Sevenless homolog (SOS) promoted Ras activation by increasing membrane dwell time of SOS (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2019.

claim: Increased dwell time of signaling effectors by condensation may be a general mechanism to fully activate a signaling pathway while ensuring signaling specificity.
source: Both cases suggest that increased dwell time of signaling effectors by condensation may be a general mechanism to fully activate a signaling pathway while at the same time ensuring signaling specificity.
evidence: This is inferred from observations of multiple signaling systems.

claim: EGFR is frequently mutated or overexpressed in cancer cells.
source: EGFR is frequently mutated or overexpressed in cancer cells (Sigismund et al., 2018) and abnormal activation of Ras in the EGFR pathway results in pro-tumorigenic proliferation and migration (Martinelli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sigismund et al., 2018.

claim: Abnormal activation of Ras in the EGFR pathway results in pro-tumorigenic proliferation and migration.
source: EGFR is frequently mutated or overexpressed in cancer cells (Sigismund et al., 2018) and abnormal activation of Ras in the EGFR pathway results in pro-tumorigenic proliferation and migration (Martinelli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martinelli et al., 2017.

claim: Activation of EGFR is associated with membrane-bound clusters.
source: Given that activation of EGFR is associated with membrane-bound clusters (Liang et al., 2018), it is very likely that EGFR condensate formation regulates pro-tumorigenic activation of Ras.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liang et al., 2018.

claim: EGFR condensate formation likely regulates pro-tumorigenic activation of Ras.
source: Given that activation of EGFR is associated with membrane-bound clusters (Liang et al., 2018), it is very likely that EGFR condensate formation regulates pro-tumorigenic activation of Ras.
evidence: This is inferred from the association of EGFR with membrane clusters and the role of Ras in tumorigenesis.

claim: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway is deregulated in many cancers in the colon, gastric, breast, and liver.
source: One example is the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, which governs numerous cell fate decisions during animal development, and is deregulated in many cancers in the colon, gastric, breast, and liver (Sanchez-Vega et al., 2018; Schaefer and Peifer, 2019; Zhan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sanchez-Vega et al., 2018; Schaefer and Peifer, 2019; Zhan et al., 2017.

claim: In the absence of a Wnt signal, β-catenin is phosphorylated by a destruction complex and subsequently degraded by the proteasome.
source: In the absence of a Wnt signal, β-catenin is phosphorylated by a destruction complex, which is composed of Axin, tumor suppressor adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) and some additional components. Phosphorylated β-catenin is recognized by the Cullin-based E3 Ligase SCFβTrCP, promoting the degradation of β-catenin by the proteasome (Stamos and Weis, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stamos and Weis, 2013.

claim: Binding of Wnt to its cell surface receptors triggers the assembly of a signalosome, which is mediated by the Dishevelled (Dvl) protein.
source: Importantly, binding of Wnt to its cell surface receptors triggers the assembly of a signalosome, which is mediated by the Dishevelled (Dvl) protein (Bienz, 2020; Bilic et al., 2007; Fiedler et al., 2011; Gammons et al., 2016; Madrzak et al., 2015; Schwarz-Romond et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bienz, 2020; Bilic et al., 2007; Fiedler et al., 2011; Gammons et al., 2016; Madrzak et al., 2015; Schwarz-Romond et al., 2007.

claim: The Axin complex is recruited to the signalosome, which destabilizes the destruction complex and blocks the phosphorylation of β-catenin.
source: The Axin complex is subsequently recruited to the signalosome, which destabilizes the destruction complex and blocks the phosphorylation of β-catenin (Stamos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stamos et al., 2014.

claim: Both the destruction complex and Wnt signalosomes have properties of condensates.
source: Increasing evidence suggests that both the destruction complex and Wnt signalosomes have properties of condensates (Schaefer and Peifer, 2019; Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schaefer and Peifer, 2019 and illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: In the absence of Wnt, Axin is found in cytoplasmic puncta which also contain APC and other destruction complex components.
source: In the absence of Wnt, Axin is found in cytoplasmic puncta which also contain APC as well as other destruction complex components (Schaefer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schaefer et al., 2018.

claim: In cells receiving Wnt signals, Dvl and Axin co-localize in puncta close to the plasma membrane.
source: By contrast, in cells receiving Wnt signals, Dvl and Axin co-localize in puncta close to the plasma membrane (Cliffe et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cliffe et al., 2003.

claim: Wnt signaling assemblies grow by fusion.
source: The assemblies grow by fusion (Kunttas-Tatli et al., 2014; Schwarz-Romond et al., 2005) and FRAP analysis further revealed that Dvl, Axin, and APC inside the puncta exchange dynamically (Pronobis et al., 2015; Schwarz-Romond et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kunttas-Tatli et al., 2014; Schwarz-Romond et al., 2005.

claim: Dvl, Axin, and APC inside the Wnt signaling puncta exchange dynamically.
source: The assemblies grow by fusion (Kunttas-Tatli et al., 2014; Schwarz-Romond et al., 2005) and FRAP analysis further revealed that Dvl, Axin, and APC inside the puncta exchange dynamically (Pronobis et al., 2015; Schwarz-Romond et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pronobis et al., 2015; Schwarz-Romond et al., 2005.

claim: The signaling activity of Dvl is strongly correlated with the ability to form puncta.
source: Importantly, the signaling activity of Dvl is strongly correlated with the ability to form these puncta (Schwarz-Romond et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwarz-Romond et al., 2005.

claim: Puncta assembly is critical for destruction complex function.
source: Similarly, puncta assembly is critical for destruction complex function (Faux et al., 2008; Schaefer and Peifer, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Faux et al., 2008; Schaefer and Peifer, 2019.

claim: APC is required for puncta assembly and cooperates with Axin to ensure efficient β-catenin destruction.
source: APC is required for puncta assembly and cooperates with Axin to ensure efficient β-catenin destruction (Pronobis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pronobis et al., 2015.

claim: Mutations in APC initiate >80% of colon cancers.
source: Strikingly, mutations in APC, initiate >80% of colon cancers (Zhang and Shay, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang and Shay, 2017.

claim: β-catenin uses its IDRs to selectively partition into transcriptional condensates at super-enhancers.
source: Reports showed that β-catenin uses its IDRs to selectively partition into transcriptional condensates at super-enhancers (Zamudio et al., 2019; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zamudio et al., 2019 and listed in Table 1.

claim: Some cancer-related mutations in β-catenin prevent phosphorylation-dependent ubiquitination of β-catenin, leading to accumulation of β-catenin in the nucleus.
source: Some cancer-related mutations in β-catenin prevent phosphorylation-dependent ubiquitination of β-catenin, leading to accumulation of β-catenin in the nucleus (Kim and Jeong, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim and Jeong, 2019.

claim: In cancer cells, β-catenin may form aberrant nuclear condensates because of elevated protein levels and this may promote tumorigenesis through widespread changes in gene expression.
source: This suggests that in cancer cells, β-catenin may form aberrant nuclear condensates because of elevated protein levels and that this may promote tumorigenesis through widespread changes in gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of β-catenin accumulation and its role in transcriptional condensates.

claim: p62 acts as a receptor targeting cargo for degradation but is also itself degraded by autophagy.
source: The regulation of p62 is complex as p62 acts as a receptor targeting cargo for degradation but it is also itself degraded by autophagy (Sánchez-Martín et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sánchez-Martín et al., 2019.

claim: When autophagy is impaired, p62 accumulates and can activate downstream signaling pathways including mTORC1, NF-κB, and NRF2.
source: However, when autophagy is impaired, p62 accumulates and can activate downstream signaling pathways including mTORC1, NF-κB, and NRF2, influencing nutrient sensing, inflammation and the oxidative stress response, which may all affect tumorigenesis (Moscat et al., 2016; Sánchez-Martín et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moscat et al., 2016; Sánchez-Martín et al., 2019.

claim: Accumulation of p62 has been shown to accelerate the development of pancreatic cancer through activating NF-κB and NRF2 signaling.
source: For instance, accumulation of p62 has been shown to accelerate the development of pancreatic cancer through activating NF-κB and NRF2 signaling (Duran et al., 2008; Ling et al., 2012; Todoric et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duran et al., 2008; Ling et al., 2012; Todoric et al., 2017.

claim: p62 accumulation in chronically damaged liver cells activates NRF2 and promotes the development of hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: Similarly, p62 accumulation in chronically damaged liver cells activates NRF2 and promotes the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (Nakagawa et al., 2014; Umemura et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakagawa et al., 2014; Umemura et al., 2016.

claim: p62 assembles together with ubiquitinated proteins into condensates, and the formed condensates are subsequently engulfed by autophagosomes and degraded.
source: Intriguingly, recent studies have shown that p62 assembles together with ubiquitinated proteins into condensates (Table 1), and the formed condensates are subsequently engulfed by autophagosomes and degraded (Sun et al., 2018; Zaffagnini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sun et al., 2018; Zaffagnini et al., 2018 and listed in Table 1.

claim: p62 assembles into condensates together with mutant KEAP1 proteins and the transcription factor NRF2, thereby affecting NRF2-driven transcription.
source: Another study found that p62 assembles into condensates together with mutant KEAP1 proteins and the transcription factor NRF2, thereby affecting NRF2-driven transcription (Cloer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cloer et al., 2018.

claim: SGs are formed by phase separation.
source: SGs, a type of stress-induced membraneless compartment, promote cell survival during stress conditions and have been shown to be formed by phase separation (Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Molliex et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Sanders et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Molliex et al., 2015; Patel et al., 2015; Sanders et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2020.

claim: Cancer cells usually exist in a unique microenvironment characterized by hypoxia, high levels of reactive oxygen species, and nutrient starvation.
source: Due to the high metabolic demands of proliferation, cancer cells usually exist in a unique microenvironment characterized by hypoxia, high levels of reactive oxygen species, and nutrient starvation (Ackerman and Simon, 2014), conditions which activate the cellular stress response and trigger SG assembly.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ackerman and Simon, 2014.

claim: The assembly of SG promotes cancer cell adaption to adverse microenvironments and enhances cancer cell resistance to apoptosis by accumulating anti-apoptosis molecules.
source: The assembly of SG promotes cancer cell adaption to adverse microenvironments and enhances cancer cell resistance to apoptosis by accumulating anti-apoptosis molecules (Arimoto et al., 2008; Thedieck et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arimoto et al., 2008; Thedieck et al., 2013.

claim: KRAS mutations are detected in many highly malignant cancers, such as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, colorectal adenocarcinoma, and lung adenocarcinoma.
source: KRAS mutations are detected in many highly malignant cancers, such as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, colorectal adenocarcinoma, and lung adenocarcinoma (Cox et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cox et al., 2014.

claim: SG assembly is induced in transformed or cancerous cells expressing mutant Kras, and this depends on the secretion of 15-deoxy-delta 12, 14 prostaglandin J2 (15-d-PGJ2), a lipid that inactivates the eukaryotic initiation factor eIF4A.
source: SG assembly was found to be induced in transformed or cancerous cells expressing mutant Kras, and this was shown to depend on the secretion of 15-deoxy-delta 12, 14 prostaglandin J2 (15-d-PGJ2), a lipid that inactivates the eukaryotic initiation factor eIF4A (Kim et al., 2007; Grabocka and Bar-Sagi, 2016; Table 1 and Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2007; Grabocka and Bar-Sagi, 2016 and illustrated in Table 1 and Figure 6.

claim: Inhibiting SG assembly and prostaglandin synthesis caused mutant Kras cells to be more sensitive to stress.
source: Importantly, inhibiting SG assembly and prostaglandin synthesis caused mutant Kras cells to be more sensitive to stress.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Mutant Kras establishes a more stress-resistant cellular condition through SG assembly and this confers a fitness advantage to cancer cells.
source: Thus, mutant Kras establishes a more stress-resistant cellular condition through SG assembly and this confers a fitness advantage to cancer cells and presumably also resistance to chemotherapeutics.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inhibiting SG assembly increases stress sensitivity.

claim: DDX3X is mutated in many human tumor types.
source: One example is DDX3X, which is mutated in many human tumor types (Valentin-Vega et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Valentin-Vega et al., 2016.

claim: In medulloblastomas, mutations in DDX3X affect RNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis and this causes SG hyper-assembly even under non-stress conditions, which results in impairing global translation.
source: In medulloblastomas (MB), mutations in DDX3X affect RNA-stimulated ATP hydrolysis and this causes SG hyper-assembly even under non-stress conditions, which results in impairing global translation (Valentin-Vega et al., 2016; Table 1 and Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Valentin-Vega et al., 2016 and illustrated in Table 1 and Figure 6.

claim: Deleting the N-terminal IDR of MB-associated DDX3X prevented SG hyper-assembly and reversed the translation inhibitory effect.
source: In agreement with this, deleting the N-terminal IDR of MB-associated DDX3X prevented SG hyper-assembly and reversed the translation inhibitory effect (Valentin-Vega et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Valentin-Vega et al., 2016.

claim: Deregulation of translation promotes cellular transformation and tumor development.
source: In agreement with this, accumulating evidence indicates that deregulation of translation promotes cellular transformation and tumor development (Ruggero, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ruggero, 2013.

claim: Increased protein levels of YB-1 are highly correlated with cancer progression and poor prognosis.
source: Increased protein levels of YB-1 are highly correlated with cancer progression and poor prognosis (Lasham et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lasham et al., 2013.

claim: YB-1 promotes SG assembly by translationally upregulating G3BP1 which is essential for SG assembly.
source: YB-1 was recently shown to promote SG assembly by translationally upregulating G3BP1 which is essential for SG assembly (Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Sanders et al., 2020; Somasekharan et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2020; Table 1 and Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Sanders et al., 2020; Somasekharan et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2020 and illustrated in Table 1 and Figure 6.

claim: Knockdown of G3BP1 severely impairs SG assembly and inhibits invasion and metastasis.
source: Knockdown of G3BP1 severely impairs SG assembly and inhibits invasion and metastasis (Somasekharan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Somasekharan et al., 2015.

claim: PML bodies are stress-sensitive nuclear condensates.
source: PML bodies are stress-sensitive nuclear condensates (Banani et al., 2016; Zhu and Brangwynne, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Banani et al., 2016; Zhu and Brangwynne, 2015.

claim: PML bodies are involved in transcriptional regulation, protein modification, apoptosis, cellular senescence, cell cycle progression, angiogenesis, and protein quality control.
source: They are involved in transcriptional regulation, protein modification, apoptosis, cellular senescence, cell cycle progression, angiogenesis, and protein quality control (Hsu and Kao, 2018; Mediani et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hsu and Kao, 2018; Mediani et al., 2019.

claim: The formation of the PML body is driven by PML:PML interactions and SUMOylation of PML.
source: The formation of the PML body is driven by PML:PML interactions (Huang et al., 2014) and SUMOylation of PML, which promotes the recruitment of proteins containing SUMO-interacting motifs (SIMs) to PML bodies (Banani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2014 and Banani et al., 2016.

claim: PML body formation regulates PTMs on p53, which are required for full p53 activity and oncogene-induced senescence.
source: Importantly, PML body formation regulates PTMs on p53, which are required for full p53 activity and oncogene-induced senescence (Ferbeyre et al., 2000; Pearson et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ferbeyre et al., 2000; Pearson et al., 2000.

claim: In acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), PML is fused with full-length Retinoic Acid Receptor-alpha (RARA) because of a chromosomal translocation.
source: In acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), PML is fused with full-length Retinoic Acid Receptor-alpha (RARA) because of a chromosomal translocation (de Thé et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to de Thé et al., 1990.

claim: The expression of PML/RARA leads to disruption of PML bodies and deregulation of transcriptional programs that control senescence and differentiation.
source: The expression of PML/RARA leads to disruption of PML bodies and deregulation of transcriptional programs that control senescence and differentiation (de Thé and Chen, 2010; Dos Santos et al., 2013; Table 1 and Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Thé and Chen, 2010; Dos Santos et al., 2013 and illustrated in Table 1 and Figure 6.

claim: RA and arsenic trioxide induce PML body formation and this promotes p53-driven senescence, which is required for APL eradication.
source: RA and arsenic trioxide induce PML body formation and this in turn promotes p53-driven senescence, which is required for APL eradication (Ablain et al., 2013; Ablain et al., 2014; de Thé et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ablain et al., 2013; Ablain et al., 2014; de Thé et al., 2017.

claim: Defective PML body formation promotes APL progression at least in part because APL cells cannot activate p53-driven senescence.
source: Thus, defective PML body formation promotes APL progression at least in part because APL cells cannot activate p53-driven senescence.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PML body formation is required for p53-driven senescence.

claim: Aberrant PML body formation contributes to APL pathogenesis by increasing genome instability.
source: Moreover, recent work reveals that aberrant PML body formation contributes to APL pathogenesis by increasing genome instability (Voisset et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Voisset et al., 2018.

claim: PML body disruption causes chromosome abnormalities and impairs DNA damage response pathways.
source: PML body disruption was shown to cause chromosome abnormalities and impair DNA damage response pathways.
evidence: This is based on observations from studies of PML body function.

claim: Telomerase-negative cancer cells employ a mechanism known as recombination-based alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) to maintain telomere length and stability.
source: Telomerase-negative cancer cells employ a mechanism known as recombination-based alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) to maintain telomere length and stability (Bryan et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bryan et al., 1997.

claim: In ALT cancer cells, PML bodies associate with telomeres and DNA repair proteins to form ALT-associated PML bodies (APB).
source: In ALT cancer cells, PML bodies associate with telomeres, their protective sheltering proteins TRF1/2 and several DNA repair proteins to form ALT-associated PML bodies (APB) (Osterwald et al., 2015; Yeager et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Osterwald et al., 2015; Yeager et al., 1999.

claim: The formation of APBs is driven by phase separation, thus promoting the clustering of telomere repeats and telomere lengthening.
source: A recent study suggests that the formation of APBs is driven by phase separation, thus promoting the clustering of telomere repeats and telomere lengthening (Zhang et al., 2020; Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2020 and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Knocking down the PML body component PML inhibited APB formation and caused telomere shortening.
source: Consequently, knocking down the PML body component PML inhibited APB formation and caused telomere shortening (Draskovic et al., 2009; Loe et al., 2020; Osterwald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Draskovic et al., 2009; Loe et al., 2020; Osterwald et al., 2015.

claim: APBs facilitate ALT telomere maintenance, allowing cancer cells to grow indefinitely and become immortal.
source: Together, this suggests that APBs facilitate ALT telomere maintenance, eventually allowing cancer cells to grow indefinitely and become immortal.
evidence: This is inferred from the role of APBs in telomere lengthening.

claim: The ncRNA scaffold NEAT1_2 drives the assembly of paraspeckles by interacting with essential paraspeckle proteins, such as NONO, SFP, FUS and RBM14.
source: The ncRNA scaffold NEAT1_2 drives the assembly of paraspeckles by interacting with essential paraspeckle proteins, such as NONO, SFP, FUS and RBM14 (Yamazaki et al., 2018; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamazaki et al., 2018 and listed in Table 1.

claim: Abnormal assembly of paraspeckles has been described in diverse cancers.
source: Importantly, abnormal assembly of paraspeckles has been described in diverse cancers (Adriaens et al., 2016; Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adriaens et al., 2016 and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: In human hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), inflammation-related IL-6 signaling increases paraspeckle formation by promoting the transcription of NEAT1_2, which is mediated by the transcription factor STAT3 and H3K4me3 histone modifications.
source: In human hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), inflammation-related IL-6 signaling increases paraspeckle formation by promoting the transcription of NEAT1_2, which is medicated by the transcription factor STAT3 and H3K4me3 histone modifications (Wang et al., 2018c; Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018c and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Increased paraspeckle formation promotes further STAT3 activation via sequestering negative regulators of STAT3 and tumor repressors.
source: Increased paraspeckle formation promotes further STAT3 activation via sequestering negative regulators of STAT3 and tumor repressors, thus causing a vicious cycle that drives further paraspeckle assembly.
evidence: This is based on observations of the effects of paraspeckle formation on STAT3 signaling.

claim: Over-activation of STAT3 induces the transcription of various genes involved in cellular survival, inflammation, epithelial to mesenchymal transition, and cancer stem cell maintenance.
source: Importantly, over-activation of STAT3 induces the transcription of various genes involved in cellular survival, inflammation, epithelial to mesenchymal transition, and cancer stem cell maintenance (Yu et al., 2014), all of which promote tumor progression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2014.

claim: The non-coding, paraspeckle-associated RNA NEAT1 is induced by p53 in response to various p53-activating signals.
source: The non-coding, paraspeckle-associated RNA NEAT1 is induced by p53 in response to various p53-activating signals (Mello et al., 2017; Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mello et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: NEAT1 overexpression suppresses the transformation of pancreatic cancer cells, and this effect was associated with an increase in the number of paraspeckles.
source: Additionally, NEAT1 overexpression suppresses the transformation pancreatic cancer cells, and this effect was associated with an increase in the number of paraspeckles.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: NEAT1 deficiency impairs paraspeckle formation and promotes pancreatic cancer initiation.
source: Conversely, NEAT1 deficiency was shown to impair paraspeckle formation and promote pancreatic cancer initiation.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: NEAT1 has been shown to be regulated by cancer-related transcription factors, such as HIF-2α, Oct4, PML/RARA, and c-Myc.
source: In addition to STAT3 and p53, NEAT1 has been shown to be regulated by other cancer-related transcription factors, such as HIF-2α (Choudhry et al., 2015), Oct4 (Jen et al., 2017), PML/RARA (Zeng et al., 2014), and c-Myc (Zeng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Choudhry et al., 2015; Jen et al., 2017; Zeng et al., 2014; Zeng et al., 2018.

claim: PML/RARA represses NEAT1 expression.
source: The example of PML/RARA is particularly interesting, because it not only represses NEAT1 expression (Zeng et al., 2014), but also disrupts PML bodies (discussed above).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zeng et al., 2014.

claim: The oncoprotein PML/RARA promotes aberrant assembly of two nuclear condensates, PML bodies and paraspeckles, to drive tumorigenesis.
source: This suggests that the oncoprotein PML/RARA promotes aberrant assembly of two nuclear condensates, PML bodies and paraspeckles, to drive tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of PML/RARA on both PML bodies and paraspeckles.

claim: NEAT1 has been reported to regulate many cancer-related microRNAs whose target mRNAs are involved in cell proliferation, migration, invasion, metastasis, EMT, stem cell-like phenotype, chemoresistance and radioresistance.
source: Finally, NEAT1 has been reported to regulate many cancer-related microRNAs whose targets mRNAs are involved in cell proliferation, migration, invasion, metastasis, EMT, stem cell-like phenotype, chemoresistance and radioresistance (Dong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dong et al., 2018.

claim: NEAT1 promotes metastasis by abolishing microRNA-382–3 p-mediated suppression of ROCK1.
source: For instance, NEAT1 promotes metastasis by abolishing microRNA-382–3 p-mediated suppression of Rho Associated Coiled-Coil Containing Protein Kinase 1 (ROCK1) (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2018.

claim: Amyloid bodies are stress-induced storage compartments in the nucleolus.
source: Amyloid bodies are stress-induced storage compartments in the nucleolus.
evidence: This is a definition based on the characteristics of amyloid bodies.
